back: The mass of living material in an area, usually measured as dry mass.
The rate at which new biomass is produced per unit area per unit time, e.g. tonnes per hectare per year.
Light, water, temperature, mineral salts, carbon dioxide, pests, diseases and weeds.
Maize stalk borer and fall armyworm (maize), bollworms (cotton), cutworms (seedlings), locusts (maize, grasses).
Aphids (cotton, tobacco, vegetables), red spider mites (cotton, tomatoes, beans) and whiteflies (cotton, tobacco, tomatoes).
notes: Red spider mites have eight legs: they are arachnids, not insects.

front: Bacterial wilt: crops, cause and signs
back: Tobacco, tomatoes, potatoes. Soil bacteria block the xylem, so plants wilt even in moist soil; the xylem has brown streaks.
notes: No cure: rotate with non-hosts such as maize, use resistant varieties and clean seedlings, destroy infected plants.

front: Rust of maize: cause and effect
back: A fungus; powdery reddish-brown pustules of spores on the leaves reduce the area that can photosynthesise.

front: Cultural control: examples, advantage and disadvantage
back: Crop rotation, early planting, destroying crop residues, resistant varieties. Cheap and safe, but slow and may not stop a severe outbreak.
Fast and effective. But costly, kills useful insects, pests become resistant, residues on food, pollution and danger to sprayers.

front: Biological control: examples, advantages and disadvantages
back: Ladybirds eat aphids; predatory mites eat red spider mites; Bt bacteria kill caterpillars. Specific and leaves no chemical residues, and natural enemies can keep breeding; but slow, and it reduces the pest rather than wiping it out.
Combining cultural, biological and chemical control; scouting fields and spraying only when pest numbers pass a threshold.

front: How do pests become resistant to a pesticide?
back: A few pests carry resistance alleles and survive spraying; they breed, so resistant individuals become more common (natural selection).
